hiding.excerpt: Louhi, hostess of Pohyola, Northland’s old and toothless wizard, Makes the Sun and Moon her captives; In her arms she takes fair Luna From her cradle in the birch-tree, Calls the Sun down from his station, From the fir-tree’s bending branches, Carries them to upper Northland, To the darksome Sariola; Hides the Moon, no more to glimmer, In a rock of many colors; Hides the Sun, to shine no longer, In the iron-banded mountain; Thereupon these words she utters: “Moon of gold and Sun of silver, Hide your faces in the caverns Of Pohyola’s dismal mountain; Shine no more to gladden Northland, Till I come to give ye freedom, Drawn by coursers nine in number, Sable coursers of one mother!
hiding.note: Verbatim English verse translated by John Martin Crawford from Lönnrot's nineteenth-century compilation of oral poetry; not a transcript of one ancient or single oral witness.

narrativeBlocks.title: Louhi hides the luminaries
narrativeBlocks.body: In Rune XLVII, Louhi of Pohjola hides the Sun and Moon in a mountain cavern and says they will not shine until she frees them.

narrativeBlocks.title: The command to hide
narrativeBlocks.body: Source quotation (Crawford's English translation; whitespace normalized): “Louhi, hostess of Pohyola, Northland’s old and toothless wizard, Makes the Sun and Moon her captives; In her arms she takes fair Luna From her cradle in the birch-tree, Calls the Sun down from his station, From the fir-tree’s bending branches, Carries them to upper Northland, To the darksome Sariola; Hides the Moon, no more to glimmer, In a rock of many colors; Hides the Sun, to shine no longer, In the iron-banded mountain; Thereupon these words she utters: “Moon of gold and Sun of silver, Hide your faces in the caverns Of Pohyola’s dismal mountain; Shine no more to gladden Northland, Till I come to give ye freedom, Drawn by coursers nine in number, Sable coursers of one mother!”

narrativeBlocks.title: Northland loses its light
narrativeBlocks.body: The poem then describes the Sun and Moon vanishing and darkness covering Kalevala and the home of Ukko.

narrativeBlocks.title: Do not flatten the Kalevala
narrativeBlocks.body: Louhi's episode belongs to Crawford's translation of Lönnrot's compiled epic. Keep Pohjola, Northland, and this poem's sequence attached to the claim.

narrativeBlocks.title: A disruption calls for response
narrativeBlocks.body: The disappearance changes daily life in the poem: the houses become dark and the inhabitants seek a remedy.
